extracted.intended_audience: vocational-technical educators, school administrators, curriculum planners for post-high-school data processing programs (state boards, community colleges, vocational schools)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for developing, staffing, equipping, operating, and evaluating two-year post-high-school (technical) data processing (EDP) training programs, including curriculum outlines, admissions, instructor qualifications, laboratory selection, costs, and review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major program objective — prepare a technically qualified data processing technician
rubrics_metrics.description: The major objective of this two-year program is to prepare a technically qualified data processing technician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates must be knowledgeable in Data Processing technology and the conditions in which they will be working — the machine and its operation and related equipment. Specific basic functions graduates should perform: (1) Assist the Systems Analyst in problem definition and design of a logical systems approach; (2) Develop detailed Data Processing procedures, wire control panels or write programs, and document these procedures in a professional manner; (3) Develop test data and test the procedures and programs; (4) Implement the use of the system; (5) Make modifications and changes as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional program objectives and course offerings
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to preparing technicians, the program should provide: at end of first year qualification as a Unit Record Operator, orientation courses, introductory courses for managers/college/high school students, and upgrading courses for employed personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adult evening orientation classes, introduction for business/industrial managers, orientation/programming courses for college students in other vocations, introductory high-school courses, and upgrading courses for current EDP workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum time distribution (50/30/20)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper balance for technician training: 50% of time in technical specialty (Data Processing laboratory), 30% in basic background subjects (mathematics, accounting, English), and 20% in general education and electives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These related/basic courses are designed specifically to meet technician needs and are related to Data Processing throughout. This balance aims to provide both employment-essential training and education producing informed, responsible citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-hour block approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The Data Processing Curriculum is based upon the three-hour block of time approach (student spends three hours per day in the Data Processing laboratory/classroom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons/benefits listed: allows tailoring to student's needs and more individual contact; flexibility to move between lecture/demonstration/practice; effective lab utilization (two groups can share one lab); better use of technical instructor's time; flexibility to rotate students on different machines; ideal student-instructor contact; immediate laboratory practice following lecture; meets State Plan minimum of three hours per day on occupational objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical curriculum content
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical courses should teach the technology of the industry: punched card machine procedures, basic computer programming concepts, systems design, machine applications; multiple programming courses and systems courses are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming courses cover automatic coding, planning/programming for accounting/auditing/data protection, programming electronic digital computers. Courses include systems and procedures, integrated management information systems, work simplification, procedure writing, and are reinforced by field work/feasibility studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related/background course requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Related courses to provide scope and background include accounting principles, communication skills, human relations, business organization, mathematics, elementary statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting: three courses to provide understanding of business records/control. Mathematics: logic, number systems, algebra with problem solving, logarithms, Boolean algebra. Statistics: descriptive and inferential statistics. Communication skills: emphasis on clear, concise writing, report writing, presentation methods, and oral communication proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum flexibility and local adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Curriculum guide provides scope and suggested sequence but must be adapted to local needs; local advisory groups review curriculum when new programs are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor and local staff prepare course materials, teaching guides, units of instruction, decide time per topic, textbooks, supplementary materials. Curriculum contains outlines; final determination of actual units of instruction is the instructor's responsibility with advisory/industry input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous curriculum revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Curriculum change is expected and necessary because of industry's dynamic nature; the curriculum guide shall be revised each year based on instructor experience and industry review committee recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is continuous updating to keep current with anticipated industry practices; statewide review committee and instructor feedback drive revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student admissions academic prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Students entering the two-year program should be high school graduates or equivalent with demonstrated competence in high school mathematics and interest in mathematical analysis and physical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest in analytical subjects may be more meaningful than advanced math credits; prior experience indicates these factors correlate with success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student selection — programmer aptitude test and interview
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 'Programmers' Aptitude Test' as a reliable selection aid; a student should achieve at least a score of 50.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test should be followed by interviews to ensure student understands program requirements. Combine test score with instructor judgment, high school records, work records, references, personality, energies, goals, and past achievement to decide admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counseling and dropout management
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate counseling and guidance are essential to minimize high dropout rates; past average dropout was a little over 40%, a realistic target is not to exceed 30% for a two-year program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews, counseling, and setting student expectations help reduce dropout. Early and ongoing advising is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor qualifications — experience and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Data Processing instructor should have a minimum of three years of Data Processing experience beyond the learning period and have performed competently as an advanced programmer, systems analyst, or supervisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors must have technical competence, business experience, and professional education with emphasis on Data Processing. Washington's instructors averaged ten years industry experience, three years college education, and two years teaching experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor recruitment and training methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Given scarcity of qualified instructors, two approaches: (a) train professional teachers by sending them to Data Processing schools/industry on-the-job training; (b) recruit programmers/systems analysts from industry and give them summer special teacher training or in-service courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washington favored industry professionals who know the technology and then receive teacher training; 'we believe it is not only better, but easier, to teach methodology than technology.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor staffing and salary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: School system salaries are below the minimum to attract and retain qualified EDP instructor personnel; availability of qualified instructors is the key issue for program success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless salaries and retention issues are addressed, program risks failure or falling into disrepute. Strive for competitive compensation to attract industry-experienced staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory equipment selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory equipment must provide an environment that allows students to meet curriculum objectives: sufficient capacity, speed and flexibility to handle common applications, and representative of equipment in commercial/scientific/government use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unit record machines should allow normal application design and processing; configuration should be realistic and include common features graduates will encounter. Computer system should be a current model supported by proven programming systems, use common programming techniques, and preferably have card input/output. Manufacturer support for curriculum development, installation planning, and program implementation is essential. Cost, educational allowance, and funding (e.g., NDEA Title VIII) are critical factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended initial equipment list (typical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested machine models and descriptions to equip a typical laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine examples cited: 026 Printing Card Punch; 056 Card Verifier; 083 Card Sorter with Auxiliary Counter and Sort Suppression; 085 Collator; 407 Accounting Machine; 548 Card Interpreter; 519 Reproducer with Mark Sensing. Computer system example: IBM 1620 Data Processing System with Indirect Addressing, 1622 Card Reader/Punch, 1311 Disk Storage Drives. (May be installed end of first term.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory physical configuration and environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical lab size ~1,700 square feet with two basic rooms: a classroom near the main laboratory and a laboratory partitioned into unit record room and computer room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special floor construction or extensive refrigeration needed, but require good light and forced air circulation (air-conditioning probable in many U.S. areas). Floor plans and pictures demonstrate remodeling of existing space can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory realism and practice problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory configurations and machine features should allow realistic application design and processing so students learn in environments similar to those they will encounter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide common features for use in laboratory practice problems; use configurations that simulate commercial/scientific/government practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and multi-cohort use of laboratory
rubrics_metrics.description: A single laboratory and instructor can serve multiple groups by scheduling (morning/afternoon/evening), allowing more students with limited additional equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after organization, one lab can run three programs (beginning students morning, second-year students afternoon, evening special courses) with roughly 2.33 teachers equivalent to serve ~50 full-time students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation and operational costing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic cost categories: initial equipment/facilities installation and continuing operational costs. Facilities remodeling costs typically $2k–$8k; equipment valuation may exceed $200k, some schools purchased (~$100k) or rent accessories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical first-year operational cost for one-instructor lab with 20 beginning students ~ $38,500 (breakdown: equipment ~$23,000 incl ~$15,000 rental; supplies $2,000; overhead $3,000; other $2,000; plus instructor salary). Per-student cost approximately $2,000 first year and ~$1,000 second year. Second-year operational example total ~$50,000 with staffing and overhead breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program types and phasing recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Four basic training programs: (1) two-year technician program (primary objective), (2) one-year unit record operator program to be phased out in ~3 years, (3) one-to-three month keypunch training to taper off as need declines, (4) orientation and advanced specialized training for employed Data Processing personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centers may offer combinations of these depending on local needs and employer demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate proficiency expectations — breadth and depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduates should have a general knowledge of a wide range of equipment but be proficient in one particular machine; capable of learning programming of any specific machine with minimum additional training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core/family approach: teach basic principles of technology so industry can provide specialized training; some application areas may require additional mathematics or technical courses beyond core subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field study and systems experience requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a field study or work experience project in systems (feasibility studies in actual business situations) to reinforce systems and procedures instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems development and design courses should include theory/techniques, case studies, and a field assignment practice problem to provide practical systems analysis experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory and statewide review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Local advisory groups and a statewide Data Processing Curriculum Review Committee review and approve curriculum; they provide industry input and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee concerns focused on obtaining qualified instructors, recruiting qualified students, and maintaining high standards (quality vs quantity). Committee recommended use of the aptitude test, instructor judgment, and striving to ensure early graduates are of highest quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student selection — combined criteria and minimums
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection should use programmer aptitude test (minimum 50), instructor judgment, review of high school records, work records, references, and interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aptitude test is the most reliable selection aid; the test score may be modified slightly when coupled with instructor assessment and records review.
